subject: astronomy

moments.title: Bessel measures stellar parallax
moments.body: Bessel announces the parallax of 61 Cygni: 0.314 arcseconds (modern value: 0.286 arcseconds), giving a distance of ~10.3 light years. He has measured the apparent shift of the star against background stars as Earth moves around the Sun, finally settling a debate that goes back to Aristotle.
moments.takeaway: The first successful measurement of stellar distance ended 2,000 years of speculation. Stars were real bodies at real, measurable distances.

now.title: Parallax today
now.body: ESA's Gaia mission (2013-present) is measuring parallaxes for ~1.8 billion stars with microarcsecond precision — extending the reliable parallax method to ~10,000 light years. Beyond that, the cosmic distance ladder (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) builds outward.
now.open_questions: The Gaia parallax data are causing tension in the Hubble constant measurement. Are systematic errors in distance scales contributing?

reflection: Bessel's measurement was so precise it required eliminating effects (refraction, aberration, the motion of 61 Cygni itself) that astronomy had only recently discovered. Each new precision generates new categories of error to manage.
